analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to report prices and rebates to a public database with 30 days' notice of price changes.
analysis.headline: S. 1664, a drug price transparency bill introduced by Sen. Rick Scott of Florida with three Republican cosponsors, died in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Prescription Drug Price Reporting Act would have required every prescription drug manufacturer to tell the Department of Health and Human Services each year what each of its drugs costs at the wholesale level, what its average net price actually was after all discounts, rebates, and payments to insurers and pharmacy benefit managers, and how much those middlemen collected. Manufacturers would have had to report any price increase or decrease 30 days before it took effect. All of this would have gone into a public database where consumers could sign up for alerts when the price of a drug they use changes.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who would get advance warning of price increases and for the first time see the gap between a drug's list price and its real net price after rebates; employers and unions that run health plans, whose prescription spending under the plan would have to be reported; researchers and journalists, who would gain access to pricing and rebate data that is currently kept confidential.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, employers, and health plan sponsors

how_it_helps.text: Every drug manufacturer would have to report annually, for every drug sold in the U.S., its wholesale acquisition cost, its average net price after all discounts and rebates, and total payments to health plans and pharmacy benefit managers.
Manufacturers would have to notify HHS of any price change at least 30 days before it takes effect, including the old price, the new price, and the reasons for the change.

HHS would have to post the reported information in a public online database within days of receiving it, and consumers could subscribe to price-change alerts for all drugs, a specific drug, or a therapeutic class.

analysis.who_pays: Prescription drug manufacturers, which would bear the cost of collecting and reporting the data and would lose the secrecy around their net prices and rebate deals. Consumers pay nothing directly.

drawbacks.text: The bill only requires disclosure. It does not cap prices, tax manufacturers, or give the government any power to negotiate, so higher prices would remain legal — the bill would simply make them visible.

Once the federal database became operational, no state could keep or establish its own law requiring drug makers to report or publish pricing information, which could pre-empt existing or stronger state transparency laws.
The publicly posted data is limited to a defined set of fields; proprietary, confidential, and trade secret information submitted to HHS would be kept out of the public database.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to the public is real but indirect: knowing prices 30 days in advance and seeing true net prices after rebates helps consumers, employers, and researchers, and visibility is often the first step toward lowering prices, but the bill would not itself lower anyone's drug costs. The costs fall on manufacturers in compliance and lost pricing secrecy. One genuine concern is the federal preemption clause, which could sweep away state-level transparency laws in favor of a single federal baseline.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee, where it sat until the two-year Congress ended without the committee ever acting on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Rick Scott of Florida introduced the Prescription Drug Price Reporting Act in the Senate on May 23, 2019, with Sens. Susan Collins and Cory Gardner as original cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The bill's entire recorded history is that introduction and referral; no further action, hearing, or vote appears before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prescription drug manufacturers are better off because the bill died: they never had to disclose their net prices after rebates or give 30 days' notice of increases. Consumers, employers, and health plans gained no new visibility into drug pricing, and state transparency laws remained the only reporting requirements in force.

for.name: Rick Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored the reporting and public database requirements.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in May 2019 and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration or a markup.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Republicans, and the bill never reached a vote, so no record shows how Democrats or the broader Senate would have split on it.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to publish their net prices and rebate payments and announce price changes 30 days ahead, ending pricing secrecy, though it imposed no price limits. Its preemption clause also would have replaced state transparency mandates with one federal rule.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: The rebates and other payments these middlemen receive on each drug would have been totaled and made public through manufacturers' annual reports, exposing how much of the drug's list price never reaches consumers.

industries.industry: Employers and unions sponsoring group health plans
industries.note: The bill would have required reporting on prescription drug spending under group health plans, giving plan sponsors and their members better data on what they are paying.
